body.en: Chapter 3's matrix-times-vector was already an example of the more general idea in this chapter: a function between vector spaces that respects addition and scaling. Every such function on \( \mathbb{R}^n \), it turns out, secretly is multiplication by some matrix — so "linear transformation" and "matrix" end up being two names for the same thing, seen from different angles.

A function \( T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m \) is a linear transformation if, for all \( \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^n \) and scalars \( c \): \[ T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=T(\mathbf{u})+T(\mathbf{v}),\qquad T(c\mathbf{u})=c\,T(\mathbf{u}). \] A direct consequence: \( T(\mathbf{0})=T(0\cdot\mathbf{0})=0\cdot T(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0} \) — every linear transformation sends the origin to the origin, so a function that doesn't (e.g. \( T(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b} \) for \( \mathbf{b}\neq\mathbf{0} \)) is never linear, however simple it looks.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 7.1 — Every linear transformation is multiplication by a matrix

body.en: If \( T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m \) is linear, then \( T(\mathbf{x})=A\mathbf{x} \) for the \( m\times n \) matrix \( A \) whose \( i \)-th column is \( T(\mathbf{e}_i) \), where \( \mathbf{e}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{e}_n \) is the standard basis (Chapter 5, Definition 5.5). \( A \) is called the standard matrix of \( T \).

Write \( \mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \) in terms of the standard basis: \( \mathbf{x}=x_1\mathbf{e}_1+x_2\mathbf{e}_2+\cdots+x_n\mathbf{e}_n \). Applying \( T \) and using linearity — first additivity across the sum, then scalar homogeneity on each term: \[ T(\mathbf{x})=T(x_1\mathbf{e}_1+\cdots+x_n\mathbf{e}_n)=T(x_1\mathbf{e}_1)+\cdots+T(x_n\mathbf{e}_n)=x_1T(\mathbf{e}_1)+\cdots+x_nT(\mathbf{e}_n). \] The right side is exactly the matrix–vector product \( A\mathbf{x} \) (Chapter 3, Definition 3.2) when \( A \)'s columns are \( T(\mathbf{e}_1),\ldots,T(\mathbf{e}_n) \): matrix–vector multiplication is defined as precisely this linear combination of columns. So \( T(\mathbf{x})=A\mathbf{x} \) for every \( \mathbf{x} \).

label.en: Worked example 7.A — Finding a standard matrix

body.en:
\( T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2 \) rotates every vector \( 90° \) counterclockwise. Find its standard matrix.

\( T(\mathbf{e}_1)=T(1,0)=(0,1) \) (the point \( (1,0) \) rotates to \( (0,1) \)); \( T(\mathbf{e}_2)=T(0,1)=(-1,0) \).

\[ A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}. \] Check: \( A(1,1)^T=(-1,1)^T \) — indeed \( (1,1) \) rotated \( 90° \) counterclockwise.

For a linear transformation \( T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m \) with standard matrix \( A \):

The kernel (or null space) is \( \ker(T)=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n : T(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}\} \) — everything \( T \) collapses to the origin.

The range (or image) is \( \operatorname{range}(T)=\{T(\mathbf{x}):\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\}=\operatorname{span}\big(A\text{'s columns}\big) \) — everything \( T \) can actually hit.

Both are subspaces (of \( \mathbb{R}^n \) and \( \mathbb{R}^m \) respectively) — the kernel by the subspace test (Chapter 5, Theorem 5.1: it contains \( \mathbf{0} \), and linearity of \( T \) gives closure directly), the range because it's a span (Chapter 5, Definition 5.3).

For \( T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m \) linear, \[ \dim\big(\ker T\big)+\dim\big(\operatorname{range}T\big)=n. \] The first term is the nullity, the second the rank of \( T \) (equivalently, of its standard matrix \( A \)).

Let \( \{\mathbf{u}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{u}_k\} \) be a basis for \( \ker T \) (so \( \dim\ker T=k \)), and extend it to a basis \( \{\mathbf{u}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{u}_k,\mathbf{w}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{n-k}\} \) of all of \( \mathbb{R}^n \) (this extension is always possible: a linearly independent set that isn't yet a basis can always be enlarged by one more independent vector until it spans). It suffices to show \( \{T(\mathbf{w}_1),\ldots,T(\mathbf{w}_{n-k})\} \) is a basis for \( \operatorname{range}T \), since that makes \( \dim(\operatorname{range}T)=n-k=n-\dim(\ker T) \), which rearranges to the claimed identity.

Spans the range: any \( T(\mathbf{x}) \) has \( \mathbf{x}=\sum c_i\mathbf{u}_i+\sum d_j\mathbf{w}_j \) for some scalars, so by linearity \( T(\mathbf{x})=\sum c_iT(\mathbf{u}_i)+\sum d_jT(\mathbf{w}_j)=\sum d_jT(\mathbf{w}_j) \) (each \( T(\mathbf{u}_i)=\mathbf{0} \) since \( \mathbf{u}_i\in\ker T \)) — every range vector is a combination of the \( T(\mathbf{w}_j) \).

Linearly independent: suppose \( \sum d_jT(\mathbf{w}_j)=\mathbf{0} \). By linearity, \( T\big(\sum d_j\mathbf{w}_j\big)=\mathbf{0} \), so \( \sum d_j\mathbf{w}_j\in\ker T \), meaning it's some combination \( \sum c_i\mathbf{u}_i \) of the kernel basis. Then \( \sum d_j\mathbf{w}_j-\sum c_i\mathbf{u}_i=\mathbf{0} \) is a dependence relation among the extended basis \( \{\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{w}_j\} \), which is linearly independent by construction — forcing every \( d_j \) (and every \( c_i \)) to be \( 0 \).

label.en: Worked example 7.B — Kernel and range from a matrix

body.en:
Find the kernel and range of \( T(\mathbf{x})=A\mathbf{x} \) for \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&4&3\end{pmatrix} \), and verify the rank–nullity theorem.

Kernel: solve \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf0 \): \( x_1+2x_2+x_3=0 \), \( 2x_1+4x_2+3x_3=0 \). Subtracting twice the first from the second: \( x_3=0 \), then \( x_1=-2x_2 \). So \( \mathbf{x}=x_2(-2,1,0) \) — \( \ker T=\operatorname{span}(-2,1,0) \), \( \dim\ker T=1 \) (nullity 1).

Range: \( A \)'s columns are \( (1,2),(2,4),(1,3) \); the first two are parallel, but \( (1,2) \) and \( (1,3) \) are independent, so \( \operatorname{range}T=\mathbb{R}^2 \), \( \dim(\operatorname{range}T)=2 \) (rank 2).

Check: \( 1+2=3=n \) (the number of columns of \( A \)). ✓

\( T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2 \) projects every vector onto the \( x \)-axis: \( T(x,y)=(x,0) \). (a) Verify \( T \) is linear and find its standard matrix. (b) Find \( \ker T \) and \( \operatorname{range}T \).

Show solution

(a) \( T\big((x_1,y_1)+(x_2,y_2)\big)=T(x_1+x_2,y_1+y_2)=(x_1+x_2,0)=(x_1,0)+(x_2,0)=T(x_1,y_1)+T(x_2,y_2) \); similarly for scalars — linear. \( T(1,0)=(1,0) \), \( T(0,1)=(0,0) \), so \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix} \).

(b) \( T(x,y)=\mathbf0\Rightarrow x=0 \), so \( \ker T=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb{R}\}=\operatorname{span}(0,1) \), the \( y \)-axis. \( \operatorname{range}T=\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb{R}\} \), the \( x \)-axis. Check: \( \dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{range}T=1+1=2=n. \) ✓

\( T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2 \) sends \( (x,y) \) to \( (x+2y,\,y) \). Find its standard matrix.

Solution: \( T(1,0)=(1,0) \), \( T(0,1)=(2,1) \).

\[ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \] — a horizontal shear.

\( T \) has standard matrix \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix} \). Is \( T \) one-to-one?

Solution: \( T \) is one-to-one exactly when \( \ker T=\{\mathbf0\} \). Solving \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf0 \): \( x_1=0,\,x_2=0 \) from the first two rows already forces \( \mathbf{x}=\mathbf0 \) (the third row, \( 0+0=0 \), adds no new solutions).

\( \ker T=\{\mathbf0\} \), so \( T \) is one-to-one.

question.en: Practice: A linear transformation \( T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2 \) has \( \dim(\ker T)=2 \). What is \( \dim(\operatorname{range}T) \)?

solution.en: By the rank–nullity theorem, \( \dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{range}T=n=3 \), so \( \dim\operatorname{range}T=3-2=1 \).
